summary: Describes a distance-vector routing protocol for sending multicast datagrams through an internet. It is derived from RIP and implements the multicasting described in RFC 1054. It was experimental, and implementation was not recommended at that time.

eli5.summary: Like a map shared between neighbors for finding the shortest path, but for messages going to a whole group at once.

questions: how does dvmrp differ from rip
what is truncated reverse path broadcasting
subtitle: An experimental RIP-style protocol that tells routers how to build multicast delivery trees, with tunnels across routers that cannot multicast.

tldr.problem: A draft standard for IP multicasting existed, but no routing protocol was available to support multicasting across an internetwork.
tldr.mechanism: DVMRP borrows from RIP: neighbors exchange distance-vector routes, here pointing back to multicast sources, and routers use Truncated Reverse Path Broadcasting to forward datagrams only where members may exist. Tunnels carry multicast across routers that do not support it.
tldr.outcome: The memo calls the protocol experimental and says implementation was not recommended at that time. It suggests that a link-state or Reverse Path Multicasting approach might work better.

today: RFC 1075 is labelled Experimental, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The memo itself says implementation was not recommended at that time.

sections.title: What DVMRP Is
sections.content:
DVMRP, the Distance Vector Multicast Routing Protocol, combines many RIP features with the Truncated Reverse Path Broadcasting (TRPB) algorithm. It is an interior gateway protocol, suitable inside an autonomous system but not between them. It is not meant for unicast routing, so a router that handles both multicast and unicast must run two routing processes.

RIP was the starting point because an implementation was available and distance vector algorithms are simple compared with link-state ones. The key difference from RIP is that DVMRP tracks return paths to the source of multicast datagrams, so datagrams are not forwarded to the listed destinations but originate from them. The authors note that a link-state algorithm might prove a better basis.
sections.eli5: It is like a road-map sharing game, but the map points back to where each message started, not where it is going.

sections.title: Message Format and Commands
sections.content:
DVMRP rides inside IGMP. Each message has a small fixed IGMP header (version 1, type 3, a subtype, and a checksum) followed by a stream of tagged commands. Each command is a multiple of 16 bits: an eight-bit command code plus at least eight bits of data. New commands can be added by adding tags. Messages are limited to 512 bytes excluding the IP header, and a message with an error is discarded where the error is found, without undoing earlier state changes.

The subtypes are Response (1), Request (2), Non-membership report (3) and Non-membership cancellation (4). Commands set context for later ones: the address family, subnet mask, metric, flags and infinity values, followed by the Destination Address command, which lists routes. The Requested Destination Address command asks for routes, and a count of 0 asks for all of them. The Non Membership Report and its Cancel are marked experimental and untested in an implementation.
sections.eli5: A message is a short label followed by a list of small instructions, like a recipe card made of one-line steps.

sections.title: Tunnels
sections.content:
A tunnel is a virtual network between two multicast routers separated by gateways that cannot route multicast. The RFC calls tunnels a transitional hack. A tunnel has a local end-point, remote end-point, metric and threshold, and the two routers only need to agree on the end-points.

Encapsulation is weak: the router inserts a null IP option and a two-element loose source route. The first element holds the original source address, the second holds the multicast destination, the IP source becomes the local end-point and the IP destination becomes the remote end-point. The far router restores the original addresses and removes the options. Because the source address is changed, ICMP errors go to the multicast router and not to the originating host. A new IP option was rejected because intermediate gateways might not pass unknown options.
sections.eli5: If part of the road does not allow group deliveries, you put the parcel inside another parcel addressed to a helper at the far end, who unwraps it.

sections.title: Routing and Leaf Detection
sections.content:
Routers exchange distance-vector routes much like RIP, with poisoned split horizon: a route is sent back on its own network with a metric equal to infinity and a flag set. Full updates go out every FULL_UPDATE_RATE seconds, triggered updates are spaced by TRIGGERED_UPDATE_RATE seconds, and a restarting router sends a request for all routes. Messages to neighbors are multicast to 224.0.0.4 where possible, and sent as unicast to tunnel end-points.

TRPB builds a shortest reverse-path tree from each source network. Pruning removes interfaces that are not on the tree, and the tree is truncated at leaf networks that have no group members. Poisoned routes act as votes that a neighbor depends on an interface, and a hold down timer of LEAF_TIMEOUT seconds decides which interfaces are leaves. The RFC also covers neighbor tracking and local group membership: a designated router, the one with the lowest IP address, sends IGMP membership requests to 224.0.0.1 every QUERY_RATE seconds.
sections.eli5: Neighbors say which roads they use to reach the sender. Roads nobody uses, and dead ends with no listeners, get skipped.

sections.title: Forwarding Multicast Datagrams
sections.content:
For each arriving datagram, the router drops it if the IP TTL is less than 2, if there is no route to the source, or if it did not arrive on the next-hop interface toward the source. Tunneled datagrams are first unwrapped. Datagrams for groups 224.0.0.0 and 224.0.0.1 are not forwarded.

Otherwise, the router forwards out each interface in the route's child list that is not a leaf or that has members of the destination group, provided the TTL is greater than that interface's threshold. The TTL is decreased by 1 on each copy. Thresholds let edge routers keep most multicast traffic inside a network by requiring a large TTL to leave it. Route entries keep child and leaf lists, which can be bitmaps, and dominant and subordinate router addresses per interface.
sections.eli5: A router copies a message only onto roads that lead away from the sender and that either have listeners or might lead to other routers.

sections.title: Timers and Configuration
sections.content:
The RFC lists named timers in seconds. FULL_UPDATE_RATE is 60, TRIGGERED_UPDATE_RATE is 5 and QUERY_RATE is 120. The others are formulas: MEMBERSHIP_TIMEOUT = 2 * QUERY_RATE + 20, LEAF_TIMEOUT = 2 * FULL_UPDATE_RATE + 5, NEIGHBOR_TIMEOUT = 4 * FULL_UPDATE_RATE, EXPIRATION_TIMEOUT = 2 * FULL_UPDATE_RATE and GARBAGE_TIMEOUT = 4 * FULL_UPDATE_RATE.

The default infinity is 16, and a smaller infinity shortens counting-to-infinity in small, well-connected networks. A router should be configurable with tunnel descriptions and, for each physical interface, a metric, infinity, threshold and subnet mask. If no threshold is given, the metric is the default. The conclusion says an implementation was done and being tested, and that NMR messages are designed to support the Reverse Path Multicasting algorithm.
sections.eli5: Routers have a few stopwatches that say how often to chat and how long to wait before assuming a neighbor or a road is gone.

fields.name: Subtype
fields.desc: Response, Request, Non-membership report or Non-membership cancellation.

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: 16-bit one's complement of the one's complement sum of the message, excluding the IP header.

items.label: AFI
items.desc: Address family for later addresses; 2 is IP.

items.label: Subnetmask
items.desc: Subnet mask for later routes; count is 0 or 1.

items.label: Flags0
items.desc: Bit 7 unreachable, bit 6 split horizon concealed route.

items.label: DA
items.desc: Destination address list that defines routes.

items.label: RDA
items.desc: Destinations whose routes are requested; count 0 means all.

items.label: NMR
items.desc: Non-membership reports with hold down times; experimental.
